subject: Archaeology
title: Plague DNA: Ancient Pandemics
description: A quick, practical guide to Plague DNA: Ancient Pandemics.

hook.text: Scientists pulled plague DNA from 5,000-year-old teeth. The killer bacterium is ancient.

buildup.text: Yersinia pestis has been found in remains across Eurasia dating back to 3000 BCE.

discovery.text: Early strains lacked flea transmission genes. They spread person-to-person, not through rats.

twist.text: A plague pandemic may explain mysterious population crashes in Neolithic Europe.

climax.text: Tracking plague evolution helps predict how future pandemics might emerge.

punchline.text: The plague is 5,000 years old. Teeth trapped the evidence.

quiz.question: What did ancient plague DNA reveal about early strains?
options: They were far more lethal than the medieval Black Death
Early forms lacked flea transmission and spread person-to-person
The bacterium came from the Americas and was carried east

details.summary: Scientists extract Yersinia pestis DNA from ancient plague victims' teeth, mapping how the Black Death and earlier plague pandemics spread across continents. Ancient plague DNA reveals that devastating outbreaks occurred thousands of years before the 14th-century Black Death.
details.whyItMatters: Ancient plague DNA rewrites pandemic history and informs modern epidemiology. Understanding how past pandemics spread, mutated, and killed helps predict future outbreak patterns and guides public health responses.
takeaways: Plague DNA is extracted from ancient victims' dental pulp
Pandemics occurred thousands of years before the Black Death
Ancient pathogen genomics informs modern epidemic preparedness

faq.question: How is plague DNA recovered from ancient teeth?
faq.answer: Dental pulp preserves pathogen DNA well because blood-borne bacteria concentrate there during infection. Scientists drill into teeth from plague burial sites, extract DNA, and sequence the Yersinia pestis genome. Comparing ancient and modern strains reveals how the pathogen evolved over millennia.

faq.question: What have scientists learned from ancient plague DNA?
faq.answer: Plague strains existed in Eurasia at least 5,000 years ago — long before the Justinianic Plague of 541 CE. Different lineages caused different outbreaks. The Black Death strain originated in Central Asia and its genomic evolution shows how it adapted to become more transmissible.
